Ten-year-old Samira Jahan lives with her parents and younger brother in a rented flat near the Rupsha River in Khulna, where her father repairs mobile phones in a small market stall and her mother teaches Qur’an to neighborhood children in the afternoons. She was brought to the local clinic after a school health worker suggested a general child wellbeing review, not because of any serious complaint.

Samira was born at term without complications and, according to her mother, walked, spoke, fed herself, dressed, and learned toilet habits at expected ages. She reads Bangla storybooks fluently, keeps up with class four mathematics, helps pack her schoolbag, and manages bathing and dressing without reminders. Her teachers describe her as quiet but responsive, able to follow instructions, finish classwork, and take part in group reading.

At home she can sit through homework after Maghrib without constantly leaving her chair, and she is not known to fidget excessively or interrupt others. Her mother says Samira may daydream when tired, but she usually completes tasks if given clear instructions. She does not have frequent tantrums, fighting, stealing, bullying, or destructive behavior; when upset with her brother over shared crayons, she usually complains to her mother rather than hitting him. Neighbors know her as polite, and the school has not reported defiance or aggression.

Samira has not been persistently sad, irritable, fearful, or withdrawn. She still enjoys drawing boats, playing ludo with cousins, and watching cartoons on Fridays. She does not avoid school, markets, family visits, or prayer gatherings, and she has not been repeatedly complaining of headaches, stomach pain, or other sickness without cause. When gently asked, she denies thoughts of harming herself or wishing she were dead, and her parents have never noticed self-injury, alarming statements, or unsafe behavior.

There is no history of seizures, fainting spells, substance use, intoxication, or other mental or neurological illness. The family home is modest but stable; there has been no domestic violence, maltreatment, recent frightening incident, displacement, or severe family crisis. Both parents appear attentive and emotionally available, with no signs of depression, alcohol or drug problems, or other conditions interfering with caregiving.

Samira has regular chances to play and communicate: most evenings she skips rope in the courtyard with two girls from the next building, chats with her grandmother by phone, and helps her brother practice rhymes. She attends Shapla Government Primary School regularly, arriving by rickshaw with a neighbor’s daughter. Her teacher says she is included in class activities, has friends to sit with at tiffin, is not being teased or bullied, and participates in lessons without refusal or fear.

Four-year-old Maisha Karim lives with her parents in a rented flat near the Karnaphuli EPZ in Chattogram, where her mother stitches garments and her father drives a CNG in the evenings. Maisha was born at term in a clinic in Agrabad and had no major illness as an infant, but her parents noticed early that she was slower than her cousins: she sat without support close to 10 months, walked after her second birthday, and still struggles to climb stairs without holding both the railing and her mother’s hand. She speaks mostly in single words like “pani” and “amma,” rarely joins two words, and often pulls adults by the hand instead of asking. At the neighbourhood playgroup, she prefers lining up bottle caps rather than playing with other children, becomes upset when routines change, and needs help with feeding, dressing, and using the toilet far more than other children her age.

Her family meals are regular despite their modest income: rice, dal, egg or fish most days, vegetables from the bazaar, and iodized packet salt used at home. At her recent community clinic visit, she was active and well nourished, with no pallor, mouth ulcers, swollen neck, chronic diarrhoea, persistent cough, fever, weight loss, or enlarged lymph nodes. She has not had repeated ear discharge or ear pain, and there is no known HIV exposure or long-running infection in the household.

Maisha appears to see and hear well in daily life. She looks directly at her mother’s face when teased, follows a rolling red ball across the room, points to pictures on her cousin’s phone, and picks up tiny beads from the floor. She turns immediately when the pressure cooker whistles or when her father calls her name from the doorway, startles at sudden loud honking outside, and enjoys dancing when music plays from the television. Despite intact hearing and vision and no signs of nutritional or infectious illness, her delays in language, motor skills, social interaction, and self-care have become increasingly clear to her family.

Fifteen-year-old Tasnim Jahan lives with her parents and younger brother in a rented flat near the railway station in Cumilla, where she attends class ten at a girls’ high school and helps her mother in the evenings by tutoring two neighborhood children. Her mother reports that Tasnim walked, spoke, learned to read, dressed herself, and managed daily routines at expected ages; she keeps up with schoolwork, communicates clearly with adults and peers, maintains friendships, and handles bathing, prayer, meals, and travel to school without needing unusual support.

Teachers describe her as calm and attentive in class, not a child who fidgets, wanders around, interrupts, or loses materials. At home she can sit through lessons and complete sewing projects with her aunt, and her father says she is not unusually restless or distractible. She has no history of fighting, bullying, stealing, breaking things, running away, or repeated defiance; family disagreements are usually mild, and she is known in the building as polite and cooperative.

Until the past two days, Tasnim had been eating and sleeping normally, laughing with cousins, practicing for a school recitation, and making plans for the SSC exam. She has not had weeks of low mood, loss of interest, constant fearfulness, school avoidance, or frequent headaches or stomach pains. The crisis began suddenly after a classmate circulated an edited, humiliating photo of her in a Messenger group. Tasnim became intensely ashamed and frightened that her father would see it. This evening her mother found a goodbye note hidden in her schoolbag and saw messages to a friend saying, “I will jump from the roof tonight before everyone knows.” Tasnim admitted she had gone upstairs to check whether the rooftop gate was open and said she still intended to do it if taken home.

She has not swallowed tablets or poison, cut herself, hanged herself, lost consciousness, or become drowsy or intoxicated; on examination she is physically alert with no bleeding wounds or signs of poisoning. However, she is crying, refusing to promise safety, and repeatedly asking to be left alone because she believes death is the only way to stop the shame.

Twenty-two-year-old Nusrat Jahan lives in a tin-roofed house near the tea gardens of Srimangal, where she helps her mother stitch kantha quilts and attends a local college. For nearly a month during the last exam term, her family noticed she had become unusually quiet and tearful, no longer enjoying evening walks to the bazar or chatting with her cousins on the veranda. She slept badly, felt exhausted even after resting, struggled to decide simple things like what to cook, lost interest in meals, and kept saying she was “becoming useless” because she could not concentrate on her books or sewing orders. She moved slowly around the house and once told her elder sister that the future felt empty, though she clearly denied wanting to harm herself and had made no attempt to do so.

Her daily life suffered noticeably: she missed college classes, stopped helping with household work, left quilt orders unfinished, and avoided neighbors who came to visit. When taken to the upazila health complex, the doctor found she looked pale, had heavy menstrual bleeding for several months, ate little fish or meat because of family finances, and had low hemoglobin consistent with iron-deficiency anaemia. She was not using alcohol or recreational drugs, had not started any new medicine, and had no symptoms suggesting thyroid illness.

After iron tablets, dietary advice with affordable iron-rich foods, and treatment for heavy periods, Nusrat’s strength gradually returned over the next several weeks. Her sleep and appetite normalized, she resumed classes and sewing, and she again enjoyed gossiping with her cousins in the evenings. At follow-up, she said the sadness and hopeless thoughts had lifted along with the fatigue, and her family felt she was back to her usual self.

Fariha Tasnim is a 15-year-old Class Nine student from a riverside village near Chandpur, living with her parents, younger brother, and grandmother in a busy but affectionate household. She used to love reciting poems at school assemblies, helping her mother make pitha, and chatting with cousins in the courtyard after Maghrib, but for the past month she has seemed persistently sad and withdrawn, saying nothing feels enjoyable anymore. Most nights she lies awake for hours, then wakes tired and slow in the morning; her appetite has dropped, she has lost some weight, and she often says she is “useless” because she cannot concentrate on her science lessons or decide even simple things like what to wear or whether to revise. Her notebooks are half-empty, her exam marks have fallen sharply, and at home she has stopped helping with chores unless repeatedly reminded, spending long periods staring at her books without reading.

Her parents brought her to the local upazila health complex after her class teacher noticed the change. Fariha has no history of unusually elevated mood, needing very little sleep while becoming overactive, reckless, or disruptive, and there has been no recent death or major loss in the family. She reached childhood milestones on time, manages her self-care, communicates normally, and has never had persistent hyperactivity, aggression, stealing, fighting, or defiant behaviour. She is not using substances, has no seizures or other neurological problems, and takes no regular medicines; examination and basic history show no signs of anaemia, thyroid disease, infection, asthma, obesity, malnutrition, or medication side-effects.

Although Fariha sometimes says the future feels dark, she denies wanting to die or planning to harm herself. Her home is stable, without violence, maltreatment, or frightening events, and both parents are emotionally available, with no substance use or severe mental health problems affecting their care. She still has chances to play and socialise with cousins and neighbourhood girls, though she rarely feels like joining. She continues attending school, is not being bullied or picked on, and teachers say she is welcome in class and able to participate when encouraged, but her low mood, fatigue, poor sleep, and reduced concentration are now clearly interfering with her studies, family life, and friendships.

Nusrat Jahan, a 29-year-old quality inspector at a knitwear factory in Gazipur, came to the local upazila health complex because of recurring tightness in her chest, a “heavy head,” and a shaky feeling in her hands that tends to appear before busy production deadlines or arguments at home about money. She has visited two pharmacies and one doctor already; her blood pressure, blood sugar, hemoglobin, thyroid test, and ECG were normal, and she has no fever, weight loss, fainting, seizures, or signs of heart or lung disease to explain the symptoms fully.

Nusrat is worried the sensations mean something serious, and the worry has begun affecting her work. She has taken three days off this month and sometimes asks another worker to recheck her measurements because she feels too tense to concentrate. Still, she does not describe being sad most of the day, nearly every day. Her mood often improves after chatting with her younger sister, watching Eid drama clips on her phone, or helping her mother cook on Fridays, and she still enjoys saving money for a tailoring course. She has not lost interest in her usual activities.

She sleeps lightly on some nights before overtime shifts but has no episodes of unusually high energy, reckless spending, hearing voices, seeing things others do not, confusion, memory decline, or substance use. She does not drink alcohol and only takes occasional paracetamol for headaches. When asked directly, she says she has never thought of killing or harming herself and wants to stay well so she can continue supporting her family and enroll in tailoring classes after the next bonus.

There has been no recent bereavement, assault, serious accident, forced displacement, or major loss in her life. Her complaints seem to rise with everyday pressure and family expectations rather than any extreme traumatic event, and she has come mainly because the symptoms feel distressing and are interfering with her daily routine.

Md. Rashedul Karim, a 29-year-old launch ticket clerk from Chandpur Sadar, lives with his wife, their small son, and his widowed mother in a rented room near the river terminal. For nearly a month before his first clinic visit, his family noticed he was “not himself”: he sat silently after work, stopped playing carrom with neighbors, ignored his beloved fishing trips on the Meghna, and said everything felt empty. He slept only in broken stretches after fajr, lost interest in meals, and his trousers became loose after losing about 4 kg. At the ticket counter he made repeated fare mistakes, could not decide simple issues, moved and spoke slowly, and told his wife he was useless and had ruined the family’s future. He missed several shifts, stopped paying bills on time, and his mother had to remind him to bathe and eat.

At Chandpur District Hospital, examination found him afebrile, oriented, and neurologically normal. His hemoglobin, thyroid test, glucose, electrolytes, and liver and kidney tests were within normal limits; there was no sign of malnutrition, chronic infection, hypothyroidism, or anemia. He was not taking steroids, sedatives, or other regular medicines, and his wife confirmed he does not drink alcohol or use yaba, cannabis, or injectable drugs.

His wife then described a striking episode three years earlier that lasted almost two weeks: Rashedul slept one or two hours a night yet seemed full of energy, talked nonstop, claimed he would become the “king of river transport,” sold his motorbike to invest in a fantasy loudspeaker business, and tried to leave for Dhaka without telling anyone. That episode led to debt, family conflict, and suspension from work.

By the time he reached the psychiatry clinic, the low, withdrawn state had abruptly changed over the previous nine days. He was cheerful one moment and irritable the next, sleeping barely two hours without fatigue, pacing around the bazaar, calling relatives at midnight with grand business plans, and borrowing money impulsively to “buy a launch route.” Despite his pressured speech, he was not confused, drowsy, feverish, or disoriented, and his attention and memory were intact. There were no features of dementia, intoxication, or withdrawal, and the presentation was no longer explainable as depression alone. In the clinic he was loud but cooperative, made no threats, carried no weapon, and sat down when his wife asked. When asked directly, he denied wanting to die, had no plan to harm himself, and said he needed to stay alive to “build the family empire.”

Farhana Akhter is a 38-year-old woman from Patiya, a semi-urban area outside Chattogram, where she lives with her husband, two school-aged daughters, and her mother-in-law in a rented two-room flat above a stationery shop. She teaches Bangla at a local girls’ madrasa and is known by neighbors as quiet, dependable, and careful with money. Her husband drives a CNG auto-rickshaw and their household has always depended on both incomes, especially since the price of rice, cooking oil, and school supplies rose sharply.

Over the past month, Farhana’s family has noticed a striking change in her. She used to wake early for Fajr prayer, prepare breakfast, braid her daughters’ hair, and leave for school with neatly marked exercise books under her arm. For at least three weeks now she has seemed persistently low, often sitting on the edge of the bed after prayer with a blank expression, saying she feels “empty inside” and that nothing in the house feels meaningful anymore. She no longer enjoys teaching poetry, which used to be her favorite part of the week, and she has stopped attending the women’s Qur’an reading circle at a neighbor’s home, saying she has no interest in talking to anyone.

Her sleep has become badly disturbed. Some nights she lies awake until 3 or 4 a.m., listening to the ceiling fan and worrying about school fees and household debts; on other mornings she remains in bed long after sunrise, exhausted and unable to get up. Her appetite has fallen, and her shalwar kameez has become loose enough that her sister commented on the weight loss during a visit. At home she moves slowly, takes a long time to answer simple questions, and sometimes stands in the kitchen holding a spoon without remembering what she was doing. When her daughters ask for help with homework, she becomes tearful and says, “A useless mother like me cannot help anyone.” She has begun misplacing exam papers, forgetting lesson plans, and staring at pages without understanding them. Her headmistress has warned her twice because she missed classes and arrived late several days in a row, which is very unlike her.

Farhana feels deeply hopeless and ashamed. She tells her younger brother that her family would be better off without her and that she has become a burden. Twenty-six-year-old Tareq Mahmud, a quiet tailor from Shibganj in Chapainawabganj, lives with his parents and younger sister above their small roadside sewing shop. Over the past three months, his family noticed he had become increasingly withdrawn and suspicious. He began insisting that two men from the local market had installed a hidden microphone in the ceiling fan to record his thoughts, and he often covered the fan with a gamcha before sleeping. Several evenings he was seen answering voices no one else could hear, whispering back to “the announcer” who, he said, commented on his stitching and warned him not to trust customers.

When brought to the district hospital outpatient clinic by his father, Tareq was calm, neatly dressed, and cooperative, though guarded. He was fully awake, knew the date, place, and why he had come, and could follow the conversation without fluctuating attention. He had no fever, headache, seizure, recent infection, head injury, or new medication use; his pulse, blood pressure, glucose, and basic examination were unremarkable. His family said he does not drink alcohol, use yaba, cannabis, sedatives, or cough syrup recreationally, and there had been no period of withdrawal or intoxication. He had always managed accounts at the shop until recently, with no gradual memory decline or confusion suggesting dementia. He denied persistent sadness, loss of interest, guilt, or appetite change, and his parents had not seen him tearful or slowed in the way they associate with depression.

Although frightened by the voices, Tareq had not shouted, threatened anyone, damaged property, or needed restraint; he sat quietly during the visit and answered questions after brief pauses. He had not shown a week of elevated mood, excessive energy, grand plans, reckless spending, sexual disinhibition, or decreased need for sleep—if anything, he slept lightly because he was listening for the voices. When asked directly, he denied wanting to die, harming himself, or having a plan to end his life, and his family confirmed there were no attempts, farewell messages, or access to pesticides kept at home. The clinician explained to Tareq and his father that these experiences were consistent with psychosis, discussed safety and family support, and planned to start one low-dose antipsychotic with close follow-up for benefit, adherence, and side effects while encouraging him to keep helping at the tailor shop as much as he could.

He remained acutely agitated when staff approached too quickly, once pushing away a tray because he believed it contained poison, though he did not strike anyone when spoken to calmly. Mohammad Tareq Hasan, a 32-year-old launch engine helper from Char Fasson in Bhola, came to the upazila health complex with his elder cousin after a tense family argument about debts. He was sitting upright, alert, and neatly answering questions; his speech was normal in pace and volume, his eyes stayed open, and he walked steadily without drowsiness, slurring, extreme lethargy, or signs of intoxication. He was not pacing, shouting, sweating, trembling, or restless, and although he looked ashamed, he remained calm and cooperative. He knew his name, the date, where he was, and why his cousin had brought him.

For the past three years Tareq has smoked cigarettes heavily and used yaba tablets, first during overnight river trips to stay awake and later almost every day. In recent months he has needed more tablets to feel the same effect, thinks about them throughout the day, and has repeatedly failed to stop despite quarrels with his wife and warnings from his employer. When he tries to go without them, he becomes irritable, sleepless, and gets body aches and intense cravings, so he usually borrows money to buy more.

That morning his wife found him quietly putting a length of nylon rope into his work bag after he had said, “Tonight after everyone sleeps, I’ll finish this near the cowshed.” He admitted to the health worker that he had been thinking about hanging himself for the past week and had chosen the beam behind their house because he believed his debts and drug use had ruined his family. He had not yet harmed himself: there were no cuts or bleeding, no pesticide or medicine ingestion, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, and no extreme lethargy. His cousin brought the rope along and said no tablets, blades, or pesticides were found on him.

Tareq has no history of epilepsy, psychosis, or adolescent behavioral disorder, but his yaba and tobacco use has clearly become a substance use disorder needing care. He denies long-standing sadness, panic attacks, or hearing voices, and he has continued going to the launch ghat most days when work is available. He has not been repeatedly visiting doctors for unexplained physical complaints, does not take medicines to numb emotional pain, and is not seeking help again and again for distress; this visit happened because his family discovered the rope and plan. He also has no chronic pain—only occasional tiredness after work that settles with rest.

Thirty-two-year-old Nusrat Jahan lives in a rented flat near Shibbari Mor in Khulna with her husband and their five-year-old daughter. She works as a quality checker in a small shrimp-processing office and is known by coworkers for being punctual and talkative during tea breaks. Her elder sister brought her to the local clinic after Nusrat cried during a family dispute about money and said, “I feel exhausted by everyone’s pressure,” which frightened the family.

At the clinic, Nusrat was alert, neatly dressed, and able to describe the incident clearly. There was no smell of chemicals or alcohol, no drowsiness, vomiting, bleeding, injury marks, or loss of consciousness. She had not taken extra tablets, poison, or harmed herself; she said she had come straight from work after her sister insisted. She denied having any current wish to die, any plan to hurt herself, or access preparations such as saving pills or buying poison. She was upset about the argument but calm, cooperative, and not agitated or aggressive.

When asked carefully, Nusrat said she had never attempted self-harm, and in the past month she had not had thoughts or plans of suicide or self-injury. She described the family stress as “temporary tension,” not hopelessness. She sleeps about seven hours most nights, eats normally, enjoys watching dramas with her daughter, and continues attending work and managing household tasks. She has no history of depression treatment, psychosis, seizures, or substance use; she does not drink alcohol or use yaba, cannabis, or sedatives. She has no chronic back, joint, abdominal, or headache pain, only occasional tiredness after long shifts that resolves with rest.

Nusrat had not been repeatedly visiting doctors for vague physical complaints and had not been taking sleeping pills, painkillers, or herbal sedatives to cope with emotions. She agreed to let her sister and husband check in with her over the next few days, and she accepted a follow-up call from the clinic mainly for reassurance and support while the family tension settles.

Shafiqur Rahman, a 37-year-old mechanic at a rickshaw garage near Rupatali bus stand in Barishal, was brought to the upazila health complex by his elder sister after a heated family dispute over unpaid loan installments. He was sitting rigidly, clutching his prayer cap, and admitted in a low voice that he had decided to kill himself that night by drinking the pesticide kept in their storeroom, or by using the nylon rope from his workshop if the bottle was taken away. His sister had found him writing a short farewell message on his phone, but he had not swallowed anything, cut himself, tied the rope, or lost consciousness. On examination he was alert, able to answer clearly, not drowsy or intoxicated, with no smell of chemicals, no bleeding, and no injuries.

The family immediately removed the pesticide, rope, and sharp tools from the house, and his sister stayed beside him while his wife arranged for a cousin to remain overnight so he would not be left alone. Shafiqur said he had never tried to harm himself before, but the plan still felt “too close” when he imagined facing the moneylender the next morning.

Outside this crisis, Shafiqur had been functioning much as usual: opening the garage after Fajr, eating regular meals, joking with coworkers, and sleeping normally until the previous night. He denied persistent sadness, loss of interest, hearing voices, unusual beliefs, seizures, or use of alcohol, yaba, cannabis, or sedatives; his sister confirmed he is known in the family for avoiding intoxicants. He has no long-standing back, joint, abdominal, or headache pain and had not been repeatedly visiting doctors or taking pills to calm himself. This was the first time his family sought help for emotional distress, and apart from the immediate suicidal plan linked to the loan crisis, he had been carrying out his daily responsibilities.

Shamsun Nahar, a 34-year-old tailoring supervisor from Sonadanga, Khulna, comes to the upazila health complex after three weeks of sudden chest tightness, trembling, “air hunger,” and stomach fluttering whenever she thinks about delayed garment orders and rising household expenses. She has visited two pharmacies and a local doctor already; antacids, vitamins, and repeated blood pressure checks have not reassured her for long. Her pulse, blood pressure, glucose, hemoglobin, thyroid screening, and ECG are normal, and she has no fever, weight loss, injury, or medical illness that explains the episodes.

She is embarrassed that the symptoms have begun interfering with her work: she has missed two shifts, avoids supervising the cutting room when it feels crowded, and asks her younger sister to accompany her on rickshaw rides because she fears another spell. She still enjoys evening tea with her children and watching dramas with her mother-in-law, eats normally, and says she wants to “get steady again,” not disappear from life. She denies feeling persistently hopeless or depressed, has no hallucinations, unusual beliefs, seizures, alcohol or drug use, or history of mental health treatment. She is 34, not an adolescent, and her family describes her as communicative, calm, and cooperative, though visibly worried.

When asked privately, Shamsun clearly says she has never swallowed poison, cut herself, tried hanging, or harmed herself in any way; there are no wounds, intoxication, lethargy, or loss of consciousness. She denies any current wish to die, any plan to hurt herself, and any suicidal thoughts in the past month or self-harm in the past year. She has ordinary financial stress but no recent bereavement, assault, major accident, displacement, or other extreme traumatic event. She also denies chronic pain, saying her body aches only briefly after long sewing shifts and resolves with rest. Her main request is help controlling the frightening physical sensations and worry so she can return to work and manage her household normally.
